Eight o'clock in the morning.
Seven o'clock in the evening.

example.en: I eat bread and cheese for breakfast.

note: Egyptians call falafel طَعْمِيَّة and make it from fava beans; in the Levant falafel is made from chickpeas.

example.en: I drink tea without sugar.

note: As an object: شَايًا (a tea) or الشَّايَ (the tea, tea in general).

example.en: He eats ful every day.

note: Ends in a hamza. As an object: مَاءً, with no extra alif.

example.en: I'd like a tea without sugar.

example.en: I'd like a cup of coffee, please.

example.en: The water is cold.
The coffee is hot.

note: For food and drink. Hot weather is حَارّ.

note: Literally 'from your kindness'. لَوْ سَمَحْتَ ('if you allow') is just as polite.

example.en: Do you have lemon juice?

note: Also means 'glass' (the material). 'A bottle of water' is زُجَاجَةُ مَاء.

example.en: This restaurant is famous.

note: From طَعَام (food): مَـ often makes a word for a place, so a restaurant is 'a place of food'.

example.en: The menu, please.

note: Any list is قَائِمَة; in a restaurant it is the menu.

example.en: I'd like chicken with rice.

note: A collective noun: دَجَاج is chicken (the food, or chickens in general); one hen is دَجَاجَة.

example.en: I don't eat much meat.

note: A collective noun: one fish is سَمَكَة.

example.en: I'd like chicken with rice.

note: In Egypt the first vowel is often dropped: ruzz.

example.en: I would like a green salad.

note: Sound feminine plural: drop ة and add ـَات.

note: From يَشْرَبُ (to drink). A masculine noun with a ـَات plural.

example.en: The koshari is really delicious!
Chocolate is sweet.

note: In everyday speech it also means 'nice, pretty'. Sweets and desserts are الْحَلْوَى.

note: It comes after the verb and its object.

note: Also means 'thorn'.

note: Usually masculine, but some speakers treat it as feminine.

On the wall there is a photo of our family.

note: The plural شَبَاب also means 'young people, youth'.

example.en: Omar is not tall.

note: The adjective after it ends in ـًا: لَيْسَ طَوِيلًا.

example.en: Are you tall like your mother?

note: With an ending: مِثْلِي (like me), مِثْلَكَ (like you), مِثْلَهُ (like him).

example.en: I am twenty years old.
My brother is ten years old.

note: 3–10 take the plural سَنَوَات; from 11 the singular سَنَةً.

en: how old are you? (to a man)

example.en: How old are you, Daniel?

note: To a woman: كَمْ عُمْرُكِ؟ Literally 'how much is your age?'.

example.en: I'm a child, and children grow fast.
How old is your grandfather?
My grandmother is elderly.
Are you married?
This is my uncle Mustafa, my father's brother.

note: Children also call any older man they respect عَمِّي.

example.en: Sami's aunt (his father's sister) lives in Amman.
My mother's brother is my uncle.
My aunt Huda lives in Alexandria.

note: Also a warm way to address an older woman: خَالَتِي.

example.en: Khalid is my cousin (my mother's sister's son).

note: Each cousin is named through the parent: اِبْنُ عَمِّي, اِبْنُ خَالَتِي, بِنْتُ عَمِّي, بِنْتُ خَالَتِي.

example.ar: عَمَّةُ سَامِي تَسْكُنُ فِي عَمَّان مَعَ زَوْجِهَا.
example.en: Sami's aunt lives in Amman with her husband.
My uncle's wife is Lebanese.
Where do your relatives live?

note: A plural word; one relative is قَرِيب, which also means 'near'.

example.en: Yesterday I went to Alexandria.

note: It always ends in -i: amsi. أَوَّلَ أَمْسِ is 'the day before yesterday'.

example.en: Sami went to the sea.

note: ذَهَبَ إِلَى … = went to …. Arabic dictionaries list every verb in this form: the past tense, 'he' person.

example.en: We came back in the evening.

note: رَجَعَ إِلَى = came back to; رَجَعَ مِنْ = came back from.

example.ar: وَصَلْنَا إِلَى الْبَيْت فِي مُنْتَصَفِ اللَّيْل.
example.en: We got home at midnight.

note: The present tense drops the و: يَصِلُ (he arrives).

example.en: We ate fish near the sea.
Layla watched a film at home.

note: Used for watching a film or a match and for seeing the sights. The present starts with u: يُشَاهِدُ.

example.en: Sami came back by train.

note: بِالْقِطَار = by train; بِالسَّيَّارَة = by car.

example.en: I saw the sea for the first time.

note: The Mediterranean is الْبَحْر الْأَبْيَض الْمُتَوَسِّط, literally 'the white middle sea'.

example.en: What did you do on Saturday? (to a man)

note: مَاذَا فَعَلْتَ؟ = What did you do? Grammar books use the letters ف ع ل as the model for every Arabic word pattern.

example.en: We visited the Qaitbay Citadel.

note: A hollow verb: before -tu, -ta and -nā the long ā shortens to u: زُرْتُ (I visited), زُرْنَا (we visited).

example.en: I drank a cold juice on the beach.

note: Notice the i in the middle: shariba. The present has a: يَشْرَبُ.

example.en: We walked along the Corniche.

note: The final ى turns back into ي before an ending: مَشَيْتُ (I walked).

example.en: I swam a little in the sea.
Daniel photographed the castle and the sea.

note: From صُورَة (photo). The shadda doubles the w: ṣawwara.

example.en: I didn't do anything on Friday.

note: As an object it becomes شَيْئًا. With a negative it means 'anything'.

example.en: We visited the castle in the morning.

note: Cairo's Citadel of Saladin is another famous قَلْعَة.

example.ar: رَجَعَتْ لَيْلَى مِنْ لُبْنَان الشَّهْرَ الْمَاضِي.
example.en: Layla came back from Lebanon last month.

note: As a noun, الْمَاضِي is 'the past'. After a time word it means 'last': الْأُسْبُوعَ الْمَاضِي (last week).

example.en: I cleaned my flat last week.

note: Used without a preposition, the time phrase takes -a: al-usbūʿa. فِي الْأُسْبُوعِ الْمَاضِي is also correct.

example.en: I visited Amman last year.

note: السَّنَة (the year) is feminine, so 'last' is الْمَاضِيَة.

example.ar: رَجَعَ يُوسُف إِلَى عَمَّان أَوَّلَ أَمْسِ.
example.en: Yusuf came back to Amman the day before yesterday.

note: Literally 'the first of yesterday'.

example.en: I arrived in Cairo a month ago.

note: مُنْذُ comes before the time, unlike English 'ago': مُنْذُ يَوْمَيْنِ (two days ago).

example.en: I cooked molokhia for the first time.
I cleaned my new flat.

note: The shadda doubles the ẓ: naẓẓafa. The present starts with u: يُنَظِّفُ.

example.en: I read a short story in Arabic.

note: The hamza sits on alif: قَرَأْتُ (qaraʾtu, I read).

example.en: The weather was pleasant.

note: After كَانَ the describing word takes the -an ending: لَطِيفًا.

example.en: I travelled to Lebanon in the summer.

note: The present starts with u: يُسَافِرُ (he travels).

example.en: I spent a week in Beirut.

note: Like مَشَى, the final ى becomes ي before an ending: قَضَيْتُ (I spent).

example.ar: قَضَيْتُ أُسْبُوعًا فِي قَرْيَة فِي الْجَبَل.
example.en: I spent a week in a village in the mountains.

note: فِي الْجَبَل often means 'up in the mountains'.

example.en: I travelled to my grandmother's village.
It was a fun holiday.
How was the trip?

note: It can also mean a flight: الرِّحْلَةُ بِالطَّائِرَة (the journey by plane).

en: before; ago (with a length of time)

example.en: I washed my hands before dinner.

note: With a length of time it means 'ago': قَبْلَ دَقِيقَة (a minute ago).

example.en: Omar slept after the match.

note: Before a verb add أَنْ: بَعْدَ أَنْ أَكَلْنَا (after we ate).

example.en: After that I went back to my flat.

note: قَبْلَ ذٰلِكَ is 'before that'.

example.ar: لَعِبَ عُمَر كُرَةَ الْقَدَم مَعَ أَصْدِقَائِهِ.
example.en: Omar played football with his friends.

note: لَعِبَ كُرَةَ الْقَدَم = played football; لَعِبَ بِالْكُرَة = played with the ball.

example.en: Omar fell asleep on the sofa.

note: A hollow verb like كَانَ: before -tu the long ā becomes i: نِمْتُ (I slept).

example.en: I washed my hands before dinner.

example.ar: أَخِيرًا وَصَلَ دَانْيَال بَعْدَ السَّاعَة الثَّامِنَة.
example.en: Daniel finally arrived after eight o'clock.

note: أَوَّلًا … ثُمَّ … أَخِيرًا = first … then … finally.

example.ar: لَمْ أَذْهَبْ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَة يَوْمَ الْخَمِيس.
example.en: I didn't go to school on Thursday.

note: The verb after لَمْ is in the present form and ends in a sukūn: لَمْ أَكْتُبْ (I didn't write).

example.en: Daniel didn't come to the lesson.

note: حَضَرَ الدَّرْسَ = attended the lesson. The ض is the emphatic ḍ.

example.en: I didn't go out of the house.

note: خَرَجَ مِنْ = went out of, left.

example.en: I forgot my phone in the kitchen.

note: Verbs like نَسِيَ keep the ي before an ending: نَسِيتُ (I forgot).

example.en: I stayed at home for two days.
I read a short story in the evening.

note: قِصَّة قَصِيرَة = a short story.

example.en: The people said: 'Poor boy!'

note: A hollow verb like زَارَ: قُلْتُ (I said). 'He said to his son' is قَالَ لِابْنِهِ.

en: rode; got on, took (a bus, train)

example.en: I took the metro here.

note: It takes a direct object, with no word for 'on': رَكِبَ الْحِمَار (he rode the donkey).

example.en: Juha rode the donkey.
Everyone laughed.

note: People in general. كُلُّ النَّاس = everyone.

example.en: Have you heard of Juha? (to several people)

note: سَمِعَ عَنْ = heard about, heard of.

example.en: Everyone laughed.

note: ضَحِكَ مِنْ = laughed at; ضَحِكَ مَعَ = laughed with.

example.ar: ذَاتَ يَوْمٍ ذَهَبَ جُحَا إِلَى السُّوق.
example.en: One day Juha went to the market.

note: The classic way to begin a story, like 'once upon a time'.

example.en: My whole body hurts.

note: جِسْمُ الْإِنْسَان is 'the human body'.

example.en: My head hurts.

note: The hamza sits on an alif: raʾs. 'My head' is رَأْسِي.

example.en: My ear hurts.

note: Feminine without ة, like most body parts that come in pairs. Two ears: أُذُنَان.

example.en: Your nose is red. (to a man)
Open your mouth, please. (to a man)
This is my hand.

note: Feminine without ة. Two hands: يَدَان.

example.en: My leg hurts.

note: Feminine without ة. Two legs: رِجْلَان.

example.en: My stomach hurts.
My back hurts.

note: Do not mix it up with الظُّهْر (with u), which means 'noon'.

example.en: My head hurts.

note: Add the ending -nī for 'me': يُؤْلِمُنِي (it hurts me). Use تُؤْلِمُنِي when the body part is feminine.

example.en: Get well soon, Daniel!

note: Literally 'your safety'. The reply is اللّٰهُ يُسَلِّمُكَ (to a man) or اللّٰهُ يُسَلِّمُكِ (to a woman): 'God keep you safe'.

example.en: You are ill. (to a man)

note: Also a noun: الْمَرِيض is 'the patient'.

example.en: I have a temperature.
I have a cough at night.
I have a pain in my back.
My throat hurts.

note: Masculine, so: يُؤْلِمُنِي حَلْقِي.

example.en: He has a cold.
Open your mouth, please. (to a man)
Breathe deeply. (to a man)
Sit here, please. (to a man)
The pharmacist is in the pharmacy.

note: صَيْدَلِيَّة means both 'pharmacy' and 'woman pharmacist'.

example.en: This is a prescription for the pharmacy.
Three times a day.

note: مَرَّةً once, مَرَّتَيْنِ twice, ثَلَاثَ مَرَّات three times.

example.en: Do you have any tissues? (to a man)
I want to sleep.

note: The verb after أَنْ ends in -a: أَنْ أَشْرَبَ (to drink).

example.en: I am tired today. (a man)
I am happy that you are both here.
Are you sad? (to a man)
Layla is worried about Daniel.

note: Worried about someone: قَلِق عَلَى.

example.en: I am not angry. (a woman)

note: In standard Arabic the feminine is غَضْبَى (ghaḍbā).

example.en: I feel bored at home.

note: Arabic says 'I feel boredom': أَشْعُرُ بِالْمَلَل.

example.en: How do you feel today? (to a man)

note: Before a noun use بِـ: أَشْعُرُ بِالْمَلَل (I feel bored).

example.en: I am better today.

note: The same form is used for a man and a woman. Before a noun it means 'the best': أَحْسَن دَوَاء (the best medicine).

example.en: Take a tablet after food. (to a man)

note: The order is short and irregular: خُذْ (take!).

example.en: Don't forget the medicine! (to a man)
Drink tea with honey. (to a man)
You must rest. (to a man)

note: لَازِم does not change: the person is on the next verb. لَازِم أَنْ أَنَامَ = I must sleep.

example.en: I must go to bed early.

note: A little more formal than لَازِم. It does not change for the person.

example.en: Rest a little. (to a man)

note: In the order to a man the long ā becomes short: اِرْتَحْ.

example.en: The body needs rest.
Health comes first!

note: بِصِحَّة جَيِّدَة = in good health.

example.en: This is my advice.
Sleep well! (to a man)

note: The noun is النَّوْم (sleep): قَبْلَ النَّوْم = before bed.

example.en: No, it is not necessary.
I love sport.
The ball is coming!
I like playing football.

note: Literally 'the ball of the foot'. Basketball is كُرَةُ السَّلَّة, 'the ball of the basket'.

example.en: Omar plays in the school team.
Team one: Omar and me.
We meet at the pitch.
Don't run too much. (to a man)

note: The middle vowel is u, so the order starts with u: اُرْكُضْ (run!).

example.en: I'm going to score a goal!

note: Also 'aim, target' in everyday language.

example.en: Sami swims at the club.

note: The sport is السِّبَاحَة (swimming).

example.ar: يَجِبُ أَنْ أَمْشِيَ قَبْلَ أَنْ أَرْكُضَ.
example.en: I must walk before I run.
I haven't written the homework yet.

note: Don't confuse it with بَعْدَ (after): بَعْدُ ends in -u and comes at the end of the sentence.

example.en: I will call my sister in the evening.

note: The short form is سَـ, written joined to the verb: سَأَزُورُ (I will visit). سَوْفَ is a separate word and sounds a little more formal.

example.en: I will visit the pyramids the day after tomorrow.

note: Literally 'after tomorrow'. After a preposition غَدًا (tomorrow) becomes غَدٍ.

example.en: Do you have a plan for tomorrow? (to a woman)
Layla is busy tomorrow.

note: Also used for a phone line or a seat that is taken.

example.en: I will meet my cousin.

example.ar: عِنْدِي مَوْعِد مَعَ الطَّبِيبَة يَوْمَ الثُّلَاثَاء.
example.en: I have an appointment with the doctor on Tuesday.
When will you revise the lessons? (to a group)

note: Use it for the past and the future alike.

example.en: The place will be crowded later.
I will call my sister in the evening.

note: The person you call comes after bi- (lit. 'connects with'): attaṣilu bi-ukhtī.

example.en: I will revise the lessons tomorrow afternoon.
What will you do at the weekend? (to a man)

note: Literally 'the end of the week'. In Egypt the weekend is Friday and Saturday.

example.en: I won't go to bed late tonight.

note: The verb after لَنْ ends in -a, as after أَنْ: لَنْ أَنَامَ. Never say لَا سَأَنَامُ.

example.ar: النُّزْهَة بِالْفُلُوكَة هَادِئَة وَجَمِيلَة فِي الْمَسَاء.
example.en: A felucca trip is calm and lovely in the evening.

example.ar: نَسْتَطِيعُ أَنْ نَرْكَبَ مَرْكَبًا عَلَى النَّهْر.
example.en: We can take a boat on the river.

note: The great river of Egypt is النِّيل (the Nile).

example.en: We will take a small boat on the Nile.

note: You 'ride' a boat in Arabic, as you ride a bus: يَرْكَبُ.

example.ar: نَسْتَطِيعُ أَنْ نَرْكَبَ مَرْكَبًا عَلَى النَّهْر.
example.en: We can take a boat on the river.

note: Followed by أَنْ + a verb ending in -a: أَسْتَطِيعُ أَنْ أَمْشِيَ (I can walk).

example.en: A great idea!
Layla will stay at home.
This pyramid is very big and very old.

note: The pyramids of Giza are simply called الْأَهْرَام (the pyramids).

example.en: I'm completely ready. (a man)

example.ar: شُكْرًا عَلَى الدَّعْوَة، سَآتِي بِكُلِّ سُرُور.
example.en: Thank you for the invitation; I'll come with pleasure.
The party is at my home in Zamalek.
Friday is my birthday.

note: Literally 'feast of birth'. The possessive ending goes on the last word: عِيدُ مِيلَادِي (my birthday).

example.en: I'm inviting you to my birthday party. (to a man)

note: After أَنْ or لِـ the final و takes an -a: لِأَدْعُوَكَ (to invite you).

example.en: I can buy a big cake.

example.ar: أُمِّي سَتَأْتِي مِنْ بَيْرُوت لِتَصْنَعَ الْكَعْكَة، مَعَ الشُّمُوع طَبْعًا.
example.en: My mother is coming from Beirut to make the cake, with candles of course.

example.ar: نَحْتَفِلُ بِعِيدِ مِيلَادِ لَيْلَى يَوْمَ الْجُمُعَة.
example.en: We're celebrating Layla's birthday on Friday.

note: The occasion comes after bi- (with): naḥtafilu bi-ʿīdi mīlādihā.

example.ar: شُكْرًا عَلَى الدَّعْوَة، سَآتِي بِكُلِّ سُرُور.
example.en: Thank you for the invitation; I'll come with pleasure.

note: The warm way to say yes to an invitation or a request.

example.en: And what's your address? (to a woman)

example.ar: سَيَكُونُ عِنْدَنَا خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ ضَيْفًا تَقْرِيبًا.
example.en: We'll have about fifteen guests.
What's the weather like today?

note: طَقْس is the weather in general, as in a forecast. جَوّ is the weather around you, and also 'air, atmosphere'.

example.en: It's hot and sunny in Cairo.

example.ar: عِنْدَنَا رِيَاح قَوِيَّة وَمَطَر كُلَّ يَوْم.
example.en: We have strong winds and rain every day.
It rains a lot in winter.

note: The verb is feminine because 'the sky' (as-samāʾ) is understood: the sky rains.

example.en: I love the sun and warm weather.

note: شَمْس is feminine, and it starts with a sun letter: الشَّمْس is said ash-shams.

example.en: Today it's sunny.
Yesterday it was cold and cloudy.

example.ar: عِنْدَنَا رِيَاح قَوِيَّة وَمَطَر كُلَّ يَوْم.
example.en: We have strong winds and rain every day.

note: In weather talk the plural رِيَاح (winds) is the usual word. Like other plurals of things it takes feminine words: رِيَاح قَوِيَّة.

example.ar: الْجَوّ هُنَاكَ دَافِئ حَتَّى فِي الشِّتَاء.
example.en: The weather there is warm even in winter.

example.ar: سَتَكُونُ دَرَجَةُ الْحَرَارَة خَمْسَ دَرَجَات فِي اللَّيْل.
example.en: The temperature will be five degrees at night.

note: دَرَجَةُ الْحَرَارَة (the degree of heat) means 'the temperature'. دَرَجَة is feminine, so the number has no ة: خَمْسُ دَرَجَات.

example.en: Sometimes snow falls on the mountains.

note: For 'it's snowing' say يَنْزِلُ الثَّلْج (the snow comes down).

example.en: Don't forget a heavy coat! (to a man)
What's your favourite season? (to a man)

note: فُصُولُ السَّنَة are the seasons of the year. The same word is used for a class at school and a chapter of a book.

example.en: In summer the weather is hot.
I prefer autumn to summer.
Winter will be cold in Amman.
I love spring very much.
What's your favourite season? (to a man)

note: It follows the noun, and takes al- when the noun is definite: فَصْلُكَ الْمُفَضَّل (your favourite season).

example.en: I prefer autumn to summer.

note: To prefer A to B: ufaḍḍilu A ʿalā B.

example.en: Sometimes snow falls on the mountains.
Winter is mild and pleasant here.
We will travel in December.
There are twelve months in a year.

note: Before a month name you can add شَهْرِ: فِي شَهْرِ مَارِس (in March). 'For two months' is مُنْذُ شَهْرَيْن.

example.en: We'll travel to Amman next month.

note: The opposite of الْمَاضِي (last). It agrees like any adjective: الشَّهْرَ الْقَادِمَ (next month), السَّنَةَ الْقَادِمَةَ (next year).

example.ar: وَفِي يَنَايِر؟ هَلْ عِنْدَكَ خُطَّة لِلسَّنَة الْجَدِيدَة؟
example.en: And in January? Do you have a plan for the New Year? (to a man)

note: The month names in this lesson are the ones used in Egypt. In Lebanon, Syria and Jordan January is كَانُون الثَّانِي.

example.en: Everybody understands January and February.
My birthday is in March.
Sami's birthday is in April.

example.ar: فِي أُكْتُوبَر وَمَايُو يَكُونُ الْجَوّ لَطِيفًا فِي الْقَاهِرَة.
example.en: In October and May the weather is pleasant in Cairo.
I'll go back to Beirut in June.

note: Don't mix up يُونْيُو (June, with n) and يُولْيُو (July, with l).

example.ar: عِيدُ مِيلَادِ أَخِي عُمَر فِي شَهْرِ يُولْيُو.
example.en: My brother Omar's birthday is in July.

example.ar: فِي شَهْرِ أُغُسْطُس سَنَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْبَحْر.
example.en: In August we'll go to the sea.
The school year starts in September.

example.ar: فِي أُكْتُوبَر يَكُونُ الْجَوّ لَطِيفًا فِي الْقَاهِرَة.
example.en: In October the weather is pleasant in Cairo.
Today is the fifth of November.

note: In Lebanon, Syria and Jordan November is تِشْرِين الثَّانِي.

example.ar: عِيدُ مِيلَادِ نُور فِي الْأَوَّلِ مِنْ دِيسَمْبِر.

example.en: The weather here is colder than in Cairo.

note: The comparative of بَارِد.

example.en: Cairo is more crowded than Amman.

note: The comparative of كَثِير. For adjectives with no a-CCaC form, use أَكْثَرُ + a noun ending in -an: أَكْثَرُ ازْدِحَامًا (more crowded).

example.ar: سُكَّانُ عَمَّان أَقَلُّ مِنْ سُكَّانِ الْقَاهِرَة.
example.en: Amman has fewer inhabitants than Cairo.

note: The comparative of قَدِيم. For people's age use أَكْبَر (older).

en: taller, longer; the tallest, the longest

example.ar: هِيَ أَطْوَلُ أَعْمِدَة رَأَيْتُهَا فِي حَيَاتِي!
example.en: They're the tallest columns I've ever seen in my life!

note: The comparative of طَوِيل.

example.ar: أَجْمَلُ وَقْت هُنَا هُوَ وَقْتُ الْغُرُوب.
example.en: The most beautiful time here is sunset.

note: The comparative of جَمِيل. You also know it from مَا أَجْمَلَ…! (how beautiful…!).

example.ar: هُوَ مِنْ أَعْلَى الْجِبَال فِي عَمَّان.
example.en: It's one of the highest hills in Amman.

note: The comparative of عَالٍ (high). Don't confuse it with عَلَى (on).

example.en: Petra is the most famous place in Jordan.

note: The comparative of مَشْهُور (famous).

example.ar: الْبَحْر الْمَيِّت أَخْفَضُ مَكَان فِي الْعَالَم.

example.en: Amman is the capital and the biggest city in Jordan.

example.en: It is one of the biggest theatres in Jordan.

example.ar: الْبَحْر الْمَيِّت أَخْفَضُ مَكَان فِي الْعَالَم.
example.en: The Dead Sea is the lowest place in the world.

note: Another word for 'the world' is الدُّنْيَا.

example.en: Tourists visit Petra every day.

example.en: I'm Khalid, your guide today.

example.en: The Nabataeans carved the city into the rock.

example.ar: هَلْ مِنَ الْمُمْكِن أَنْ نَرْكَبَ الْجَمَل؟
example.en: Is it possible for us to ride the camel?

note: Careful: جَمَل (camel) and جَمِيل (beautiful) come from different roots.

example.en: My colleague helps me with the work.

note: Also a classmate. With 'my': زَمِيلِي (my colleague).

example.en: We have a meeting in two hours.

note: After a word that ends in a vowel the first i is not said: ʿindanā jtimāʿ.

example.ar: أَنَا مُتَدَرِّب هُنَا مُنْذُ أُسْبُوع فَقَطْ.
example.en: I have only been an intern here for a week.

note: The plural is used in كُلَّ الْمُتَدَرِّبِينَ (all the interns).

example.en: Can I use this computer?

note: The verb itself never changes: the person is the ending, يُمْكِنُنِي (I can), يُمْكِنُكَ (you can), and the next verb follows أَنْ.

example.en: He was the first Arab writer who won the Nobel Prize.
This is the novel (that) I read.

example.ar: هَلْ هُوَ الْكَاتِبُ الَّذِي أَخَذَ جَائِزَةَ نُوبِل؟
example.en: Is he the writer who won the Nobel Prize?

note: To win a prize is أَخَذَ جَائِزَة (took a prize).

example.ar: هٰذَا هُوَ مَعْرِضُ الْكِتَاب الَّذِي أَخْبَرْتُكَ عَنْهُ.
example.en: This is the book fair (that) I told you about.
Sami told me that the film was great.

note: From the same root as خَبَر (news). After it, use أَنَّ, not إِنَّ.

example.en: The teacher asked me whether I had understood the lesson.

note: To ask about someone: سَأَلَ عَنْ. From the same root as سُؤَال (question).

example.en: So I answered that you were a little ill.

note: To report an answer, use بِأَنَّ: أَجَابَ بِأَنَّهُ… (he answered that he…).

example.en: Music is easier for me than talk.

note: From the same root as يَتَكَلَّمُ (speaks) and كَلِمَة (word).

example.en: Is that true?

note: On its own, صَحِيح! means 'That's right!'. The opposite is غَيْرُ صَحِيح (not true).

example.ar: وَعَدَ يُوسُف أَنْ يَزُورَنَا فِي الْقَاهِرَة.
example.en: Yusuf promised to visit us in Cairo.

note: In the present the w disappears: يَعِدُ (he promises).

example.en: And in fact they're very hard!

note: فِي الْحَقِيقَة means 'in fact, actually'.

example.ar: فِي رَأْيِي، الْكُتُبُ أَحْسَنُ مِنَ الْإِنْتَرْنِت.
example.en: In my opinion, books are better than the internet.

note: فِي رَأْيِي = in my opinion; مَا رَأْيُكَ؟ = what do you think?

en: what do you think? (to a man)

example.en: Sami, what do you think?

note: Literally 'what is your opinion?'. To ask about something, add فِي: مَا رَأْيُكَ فِي الْفِيلْم؟

example.en: I believe that the internet is very useful.

note: Followed by أَنَّ + a noun ending in -a.

example.en: I think that this is a mistake.

note: A little less sure than أَعْتَقِدُ. Note the emphatic ظ.

example.en: I don't agree, Sami.

note: The person you agree with is a direct object: أُوَافِقُكَ (I agree with you), هَلْ تُوَافِقُ سَامِي؟

example.en: I agree with you; you're right.

note: مَعَكَ حَقّ (to a man) and مَعَكِ حَقّ (to a woman) mean 'you're right', literally 'with you is the truth'.

example.en: I believe that the internet is very useful.
I read a whole novel on the internet.

note: Arabic uses it with 'the': عَلَى الْإِنْتَرْنِت (on the internet, online).

example.ar: كُلُّ مَثَل جُمْلَة قَصِيرَة فِيهَا حِكْمَة كَبِيرَة.
example.en: Every proverb is a short sentence with great wisdom in it.

note: Don't confuse it with مِثْل (like). مَثَلًا means 'for example'.

example.en: Patience is the key to relief.
Choose the neighbour before the house.
Choose the neighbour before the house.

note: دَار is feminine and more formal than بَيْت. You also find it in names: دَارُ الْأُوبِرَا (the Opera House).

example.en: Whoever works hard succeeds.

note: In the present the w disappears: يَجِدُ (he finds), like يَعِدُ from وَعَدَ.

example.en: A sound mind in a sound body.
A sound mind in a sound body.

note: From the same root as سَلَام (peace) and مَعَ السَّلَامَة (goodbye).

example.en: That's a wise saying!
You reap what you sow.

note: Its partner in the proverb is حَصَدَ (reaped, harvested).
